To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) use cases are a useful technique for identifying objects in a system; (b) the role of categorizing in human cognition suggests that class diagrams can be used directly as a mechanism for communicating with users; (c) use cases should be kept at a high level of abstraction to avoid premature commitment to implementation details; and (d) the role of use cases should be to communicate and verify requirements with users, rather than to identify objects.
use cases are an effective tool for communicating and verifying requirements.
Use cases have been promoted by a number of authors as a means for capturing requirements, and for identifying objects in a system.

use cases have not yet achieved the level of maturity necessary to be considered a primary modeling construct.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
use cases are an important tool, but that they should be viewed as a supplement, rather than a replacement, for object models.
use cases are a valuable tool for communicating and verifying requirements, but that their role in the UML should be restricted to this domain.

use cases should not be considered as the primary mechanism for identifying and verifying application requirements, and that the role of use cases should be limited to that of a secondary mechanism for communicating requirements.
The main takeaway from our work is that
use cases are a powerful mechanism for capturing requirements, but they are best used in conjunction with other analysis artifacts, such as class diagrams, rather than as a primary mechanism.
the use-case concept needs to be more clearly defined and better integrated with the object-oriented paradigm.
